alpha.definition: A position where the two hands are at opposite grid points (180 degrees apart).
examples: alpha1: hands at N and S
alpha3: hands at E and W

beta.definition: A position where both hands are at the same grid point (0 degrees apart).
examples: beta1: both hands at N
beta5: both hands at NE

gamma.definition: A position where the hands form a right angle (90 degrees apart on adjacent grid points).
examples: gamma1: hands at N and E
gamma5: hands at N and NW

zeta.definition: A position where the hands form an obtuse angle (greater than 90 degrees). Introduced in Level 4 with skewed grid mode.
examples: One hand cardinal, one intercardinal, forming ~135 degree angle

eta.definition: A position where the hands form an acute angle (less than 90 degrees). Introduced in Level 4 with skewed grid mode.
examples: One hand cardinal, one intercardinal, forming ~45 degree angle

prop.definition: The physical object being manipulated (staff, fan, club, poi, etc.). The prop is what rotates. The hand is just the vehicle that carries it between grid points.
examples: Staff (bilateral): held at center, extends both sides
Poi (unilateral): held at one end, extends outward

bilateral.definition: A prop held at its center point, extending equally on both sides of the hand. The prop rotates around its center, which is where the hand grips.
examples: Staff
Double-ended baton

unilateral.definition: A prop held at one end, extending outward from the hand in one direction. The prop rotates around the grip point, which is at the edge of the prop.
examples: Poi
Fan
Club

pro.definition: A motion type where the prop rotates in the same direction as the hand's travel. At 0 turns during a shift, the prop rotates 90 degrees with the hand path. Also called 'prospin' or 'isolation' (because the prop's orientation relative to the center point stays constant).
examples: Hand shifts W to N clockwise, prop rotates 90 degrees clockwise
At 0 turns: orientation preserved (e.g. in stays in)

anti.definition: A motion type where the prop rotates opposite to the hand's travel. At 0 turns during a shift, the prop rotates 90 degrees against the hand path. Also called 'antispin'. Creates petal-like patterns.
examples: Hand shifts W to N clockwise, prop rotates 90 degrees counter-clockwise
At 0 turns: orientation switches (e.g. in becomes out)

isolation.definition: Another name for pro motion. Called an isolation because the prop's orientation relative to the center point remains constant as the hand moves. The prop appears to stay fixed in space while the hand orbits around it.
examples: Pro at 0 turns during a shift is an isolation

float.definition: A motion type where the hand shifts to an adjacent point but the prop does not rotate at all. Pure translation with zero prop rotation. Similar to a dash (also pure translation) but moves to an adjacent point instead of the opposite point.
examples: Hand moves from W to N, prop maintains its exact facing in space
Like sliding the prop sideways without spinning it

static.definition: A motion type where the hand stays at its current grid point. At 0 turns, the prop does not rotate.
examples: Type 6 letters (alpha, beta, gamma) have both hands static
Type 2 letters have one static hand and one shifting hand

shift.definition: A hand movement to an adjacent grid point (90 degrees around the grid). The prop behavior during a shift depends on the motion type: pro rotates with the hand path, anti rotates against it, float does not rotate.
examples: N to E is a shift
NE to SE is a shift
Type 1 and Type 2 letters use shifts

dash.definition: A hand movement to the opposite grid point (180 degrees across the grid). At 0 turns, the prop does not rotate — it translates straight through the center. Pure translation, like float, but covering a greater distance.
examples: N to S is a dash
NE to SW is a dash
Type 4 and Type 5 letters use dashes

hand-path.definition: The path a hand traces when moving between grid points. For a shift, the hand path covers 90 degrees around the grid. For a dash, 180 degrees across. The hand path determines the base rotation that pro and anti motions produce.
examples: W to N clockwise is a 90-degree hand path
N to S is a 180-degree hand path (dash)

turns.definition: Additional prop rotation beyond the base rotation inherent to the motion type. 1 turn = 180 degrees of additional rotation. At 0 turns, pro and anti still produce base rotation from the hand path. The turn count measures rotation on top of that base behavior.
examples: 0 turns with pro shift: prop rotates 90 degrees (base only, no additional)
1 turn with pro shift: prop rotates 90 degrees base + 180 degrees additional
0 turns with dash: no rotation (pure translation)

orientation.definition: The facing direction of a prop at any point during a step. Four possible values: in (toward center), out (away from center), clock (clockwise-facing), counter (counter-clockwise-facing). Orientation changes based on motion type, turns, and rotation direction.
examples: Pro at 0 turns preserves orientation (in stays in)
Anti at 0 turns switches orientation (in becomes out)
Dash at 0 turns: orientation changes as a geometric consequence of translation through center

step.definition: A single pictograph in a sequence, regardless of its duration. Each step represents what both hands and props do during that moment. Steps are the fundamental unit of a sequence.
examples: A 4-step sequence has 4 pictographs
Step 0 is the start position

dual-shift.definition: A letter type (Type 1) where both hands shift simultaneously to adjacent points.
examples: Letters A through V
Most common letter type with 22 letters

cross-shift.definition: A letter type (Type 3) where one hand shifts and one hand dashes. Also called 'dash letters' due to the '-' suffix.
examples: Sigma dash (Sigma-) is a Type 3 letter

dual-dash.definition: A letter type (Type 5) where both hands dash simultaneously.
examples: Phi-, Psi-, Lambda-
Only 3 letters in this type

diamond.definition: A grid mode where hands are placed only on cardinal points (N, E, S, W). The default grid mode.
examples: Standard positions like alpha1 (N/S) use diamond mode

box.definition: A grid mode where hands are placed only on intercardinal points (NE, SE, SW, NW).
examples: Position beta5 (both hands at NE) uses box mode

skewed.definition: A grid mode introduced in Level 4 where one hand is on a cardinal point and one is on an intercardinal point.
examples: Hand at N and hand at NE
Creates zeta and eta positions

pictograph.definition: A visual representation of one step of motion in TKA. Shows two props, arrows indicating motion, and position glyphs.
examples: Each letter has multiple pictograph variations
Pictographs can be sequenced to create choreography

variation.definition: A specific instance of a letter with particular starting/ending positions and locations. Each letter can have many variations.
examples: Letter A has variations starting from alpha1, alpha3, etc.
Variations differ by rotation direction and grid locations

cardinal.definition: The four main compass points on the grid: North (N), East (E), South (S), West (W).
examples: Diamond mode uses cardinal points
N is at the top of the pictograph

intercardinal.definition: The four diagonal compass points on the grid: Northeast (NE), Southeast (SE), Southwest (SW), Northwest (NW).
examples: Box mode uses intercardinal points
NE is at the top-right of the pictograph

cw.definition: Clockwise rotation direction, as viewed from above the performer.
examples: Hand path moving N -> E -> S -> W is clockwise

ccw.definition: Counter-clockwise rotation direction, as viewed from above the performer.
examples: Hand path moving N -> W -> S -> E is counter-clockwise

vtg.definition: Vertical Timing Glyph - a notation showing the relative timing of the two hands during a beat.
examples: Shows whether hands move together, split, or in sequence

reversal.definition: A change in prop rotation direction during a movement. Shown as dots on the pictograph.
examples: Prop changes from clockwise to counter-clockwise mid-beat

negative-space.definition: Passing the prop through space around the body without turning the torso.
examples: Reaching behind to execute a pattern
Using arm extension instead of body rotation

body-turns.definition: Turning the torso to execute patterns, especially for longer staves.
examples: Rotating shoulders to reach behind
Full body rotation during complex sequences
body-turns.benefit: Add movement quality, handle longer staves, create dynamic contrast

thumb-orientation.definition: Tracking whether thumbs point inward or outward on each beat to verify prop rotation.
examples: thumbs-in: starting position with thumbs toward center
thumbs-out: thumbs away from center
thumb-orientation.importance: Track rotations and check position on every beat

loop.definition: A circular sequence that returns to its starting position through transformations (rotation, mirroring, swapping, etc.).
examples: DJII (8-count)
AABB with mirrored-swapped transformation
